parts.visual:
The Pareto Principle states that roughly 80% of consequences come from 20% of the causes. Executives use this to prioritize ruthlessly.

Applications:
1. Revenue: 80% of your profits come from 20% of your clients.
2. Productivity: 80% of your output comes from 20% of your effort.
3. Management: 80% of your HR headaches come from 20% of your employees.
parts.audio: The Pareto Principle states that 80% of results come from 20% of the effort. Executives use this rule to prioritize ruthlessly and cut the busywork.

questions.question: A team has 100 features they want to build. Applying the 80/20 rule, what should the product manager do?
options: Identify the 20 features that will deliver 80% of the user satisfaction, and build only those for the launch.
questions.correct_answer: Identify the 20 features that will deliver 80% of the user satisfaction, and build only those for the launch.
questions.explanation: Perfection is the enemy of execution. The 80/20 rule prevents 'feature creep' and speeds up time-to-market.

questions.question: Listen to the VP of Sales. What strategy is being applied?
questions.tts_text: We are going to stop marketing to these 40 small accounts and focus all our energy on our 5 biggest enterprise clients.
options: Applying the Pareto Principle to revenue (focusing on the 20% of clients that generate 80% of the money).
questions.correct_answer: Applying the Pareto Principle to revenue (focusing on the 20% of clients that generate 80% of the money).
questions.explanation: Treating all clients equally is bad business. Executives disproportionately allocate resources to the most profitable accounts.

questions.question: How does the 80/20 rule apply to time management?
options: You should only work 20% of the day.
Most of your daily meetings (80%) are useless. You should find the 20% of deep work that actually moves the needle and fiercely protect that time.
questions.correct_answer: Most of your daily meetings (80%) are useless. You should find the 20% of deep work that actually moves the needle and fiercely protect that time.
questions.explanation: Busy does not mean productive. The 80/20 rule helps executives cut 'busywork' from their calendar.

questions.question: If 80% of customer complaints come from 20% of your product's bugs, what is the executive action?
options: Ignore the 80% of minor bugs and force engineering to fix the critical 20% immediately.
questions.correct_answer: Ignore the 80% of minor bugs and force engineering to fix the critical 20% immediately.
questions.explanation: Targeted strikes on the highest-impact problems yield the greatest ROI on engineering time.

questions.question: Order the words to declare a focus on high-impact work:
questions.explanation: A polite way for an executive to say 'We are not going to waste time on low-value busywork.'
